More ways to ask. First, the rest of the question-word family:

nhaltjan → how / what (of doing)
nhätha → when
nhämunha' → how many
nhäthinya(ra) → what like / how much

Nhaltjan nhe dhu? → What will you do?
Nhaltjarra walala ḻakaraŋala? → What did they say?

Notice nhaltjan has verb forms. Nhaltjan / nhaltjarra, present and past, because it's literally a pro-verb: to do-what, to do-how. It conjugates like any other verb. Imagine if English what could take -ed.

Nhätha dhu mitjiyaŋdja dhiyala? → When will the boat be here?
Nhämunha' ga ŋorranydja? → How many are there (lying)?

But here's the deeper truth about questions in Gupapuyŋu: most of the time, you don't need a question word at all.

1. Intonation alone:
Word order gives no clue. The rise of your voice does everything.
Nhe dhu buḻ'yun. → You will play.
Nhe dhu buḻ'yun? → Will you play?
Same words. Different music. The question lives in your throat, not in the syntax. (Plenty of languages do this in casual speech, but here it's the standard way.)

2. muka, the tag:
Add muka to a statement and you get the didn't-you? / isn't-it? flavour:
Nhe ŋatha märraŋala muka? → You got the food, didn't you?
Ŋayi ga buḻ'yun muka? → He's playing, isn't he?

3. bili, the did-you-already:
For have you...? / did you...? questions, front the word bili (you'll meet its whole chameleon life in a few lessons):
Bili nhe märraŋala? → Did you get it?
Bili ŋayi ḻupthurruna? → Has he washed?

4. wanha, the gentle push:
And this one is lovely: wanha (yes, the where word) used not to ask where, but to nudge someone into action. Will you...? Why don't you...? How about...?
Wanha nhe ŋanya guŋga'yurrunydja? → Why don't you help him?

Four ways to ask without asking-words. Because in a culture built on presence and shared context, a question is rarely an interrogation. It's an invitation, a check-in, a nudge. The grammar gives you exactly those textures: the rising voice, the soft tag, the already?, the gentle push.

Ask accordingly.
